interviewQuestions.question: How would you explain the architectural difference between a CPU and a GPU to someone non-technical?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd use an analogy: a CPU is like a small team of expert chefs, each capable of handling any complex, multi-step dish quickly and adapting on the fly if the recipe changes mid-cook. A GPU is like a huge kitchen of thousands of line cooks who can each only chop vegetables — but if you need a million vegetables chopped identically, the line-cook kitchen finishes far faster than the expert chefs ever could, even though any single line cook is much less capable than any single chef.

Then I'd connect it back to the actual hardware: the "expert chef" core has deep pipelines, branch prediction, and large caches to handle any single task fast (latency-optimized) — it's built to make one thing finish as quickly as possible. The "line cook" core is simple and slow individually, but the chip packs thousands of them and hides memory waits by switching between ready groups of threads while others wait (throughput-optimized) — it's built to make a huge number of things finish as quickly as possible in aggregate, even if any one of them is individually slower than it would be on a CPU.

I'd close with the practical takeaway: neither is strictly better — it depends entirely on whether your job is "one complex thing, fast" (favor CPU) or "the same simple thing, done a million times" (favor GPU), and most real systems use both together, with the CPU orchestrating and the GPU handling the bulk parallel work.

**Testing:** whether you can communicate an architectural trade-off clearly without leaning on jargon, while keeping the analogy technically accurate enough to map back onto real hardware terms (latency-optimized vs throughput-optimized).
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Explaining CPU vs GPU simply

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't you just use a GPU for everything if it has so much more raw compute than a CPU?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the design goal: a GPU trades single-thread speed for thread count, betting that a workload has enough independent, uniform work to keep thousands of simple cores busy simultaneously. That bet only pays off for massively data-parallel, control-flow-uniform problems — think shading every pixel on a screen identically, or multiplying huge matrices where every output element follows the same computation.

The moment a workload is mostly sequential, has a few large dependency chains where each step needs the previous step's result, or branches heavily and unpredictably per element, the GPU's advantage evaporates: divergent threads within a warp serialize (covered in depth in the SIMT execution topic), and its individually slower, simpler cores end up doing worse per-unit-of-work than a CPU's fast, deeply-pipelined single core running the same logic sequentially. A parser, a linked-list traversal, or most general application logic with complex, data-dependent control flow just isn't "GPU-shaped" — throwing more cores at inherently sequential work doesn't help if there's nothing independent for those extra cores to do.

So I'd frame the real decision as picking the right tool for the parallelism *profile* of the specific workload — how much independent, uniform work does it actually contain — rather than comparing raw FLOPs on a spec sheet, which measures peak theoretical throughput under ideal conditions that most real-world sequential or branchy code will never come close to achieving.

**Testing:** whether you understand that a GPU's throughput advantage is conditional on parallel, uniform workloads, not a blanket "always faster" claim, and can name concrete examples of workloads that break the assumption.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why GPUs aren't a universal speedup

interviewQuestions.question: A workload has plenty of independent parallel work, but still runs poorly on a GPU. What are the less obvious reasons that might be true beyond branch divergence?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Beyond divergence, I'd check several structural issues that can quietly undermine a workload that looks parallel on paper. First, insufficient **occupancy** — a GPU hides memory latency by switching between many resident warps while some wait on memory, but if a kernel uses too many registers or too much shared memory per thread block, fewer blocks can be resident simultaneously on each streaming multiprocessor, leaving the hardware with too few ready warps to hide latency behind, even though the underlying problem has abundant parallelism. Second, **memory-bound versus compute-bound** mismatch — a kernel that's arithmetically simple but touches a large amount of data (like a plain elementwise add) is limited by memory bandwidth, not by the number of cores available, and adding more parallel threads beyond what's needed to saturate that bandwidth buys nothing; the fix there is reducing memory traffic (better reuse via shared memory, fusing operations) rather than restructuring for "more parallelism."

Third, **launch and synchronization overhead** — a workload split into many tiny, frequent kernel launches pays fixed per-launch overhead and host-device synchronization cost repeatedly, which can dominate total time even if each individual kernel is embarrassingly parallel and fast; batching work into fewer, larger launches often helps far more than optimizing the kernel body itself. Fourth, **uncoalesced memory access** (covered in depth in the memory hierarchy topic) — parallelism at the thread level doesn't help if each thread's memory access pattern forces the hardware into many small, inefficient transactions instead of few wide ones.

The general senior-level point: "has parallel work" is necessary but not sufficient for GPU performance — occupancy, memory-boundedness, and launch overhead are all independent bottlenecks that can each individually cap performance regardless of how parallel the underlying algorithm is.

**Testing:** whether you can name concrete, independent bottlenecks beyond divergence (occupancy, memory-boundedness, launch overhead) that limit real GPU performance, showing hands-on profiling experience rather than textbook knowledge alone.
